lesson.title: The Air as a Cable: How the Wireless Medium Carries a Signal
lesson.summary: Wireless communication replaces a physical wire with radio waves traveling through open space, which makes the medium shared, unbounded, and governed by the physics of electromagnetic propagation rather than the fixed geometry of a cable.
lesson.body:
A transmission medium is simply whatever a signal travels through to get from a sender to a receiver, and for most of networking history that medium was a physical object: copper wire or glass fiber. The wireless medium removes the wire and lets the signal, an electromagnetic wave, propagate through open air or space instead. The physical layer still has to encode bits into a signal exactly as it would for a cable, but now that signal radiates outward from an antenna rather than being confined inside a shielded conductor, and that single change reshapes almost everything about how the medium behaves.

Because a wired link is guided, a signal placed on one end mostly stays confined to that cable and arrives, weakened, at the other end. A wireless signal has no such boundary. An antenna typically radiates in many directions at once, so a transmission is really a broadcast to everyone within range, not a private conversation between two endpoints. This is why wireless networks need explicit rules to decide who gets to transmit when, and why a radio generally cannot listen for other traffic while it is transmitting: its own outgoing signal overwhelms the antenna long before a faint incoming signal from another device could be heard, a problem often called the near far problem.

Radio waves are characterized by frequency and, equivalently, by wavelength, related through the simple identity that the speed of light equals frequency times wavelength (c = f times lambda). At 2.4 GHz, a frequency used by Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, the wavelength is about 3 times 10 to the 8th meters per second, divided by 2.4 times 10 to the 9th cycles per second, or roughly 12.5 centimeters. At 5 GHz, another common Wi-Fi band, the wavelength shrinks to about 6 centimeters. That difference is not just trivia: shorter wavelengths diffract less around obstacles like walls and furniture, so 5 GHz signals tend to travel in straighter lines and lose more strength when they must bend around or pass through objects, while 2.4 GHz signals reach farther and penetrate walls more effectively for the same transmit power.

Regulators divide usable spectrum into bands, some licensed exclusively to one operator, as with most cellular frequencies, and some left unlicensed for anyone to use under set power limits, such as the industrial, scientific, and medical bands at 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz that Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share. Unlicensed bands are convenient and free to use but come with a cost: because many different devices and technologies transmit in the same band, a wireless medium is inherently noisier and more contested than a dedicated cable belonging to exactly one link.

None of this changes the fact that a wireless transmission is still a signal in the sense already covered: an electromagnetic wave carrying encoded information, subject to the same physical layer principles as a signal on copper or fiber. What changes is the environment that signal must survive. Traveling unguided through open space means the signal weakens with distance in a specific, measurable way, and it arrives sharing the air with countless other signals and random electrical disturbances. Those two consequences, weakening with distance and unwanted competing energy, are exactly what attenuation and noise describe next, and they are the direct price a network pays for cutting the cord.
